title: Foundations: Piedmont Blues - The Complete Guide
summary: What Piedmont Blues is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Piedmont Blues songs: Piedmont blues is the East Coast fingerstyle tradition: ragtime-influenced, bouncy, and melodic, with the thumb keeping a steady alternating bass while the fingers dance. It's the friendliest-sounding blues.

History: Centered on the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia in the 1920s–30s. Blind Blake, Blind Boy Fuller, and the Reverend Gary Davis recorded intricate fingerstyle pieces that became the bible for 1960s folk-revival guitarists.

How the songs work: Piedmont Blues favors the keys of C, G, E, A. Common forms include Ragtime 16-bar and 32-bar forms; Blues verses with instrumental ragtime breaks. Players should master alternating thumb bass: root–fifth–root–fifth first, then syncopated melody against the steady thumb. Capo 2–4 for bright fingerstyle tone.

title: Police Dog Blues - Piedmont Blues Song Study
summary: Harmonic blueprint and playing guide for Police Dog Blues by Blind Blake (1929).
body:
Police Dog Blues — Blind Blake, 1929. Blake's piano-like guitar ragtime.

HARMONIC BLUEPRINT (study chart, key of E):
E | C#7 | F#7 | B7

This study chart uses the 'Circle-of-fifths turnaround' progression, the Piedmont Blues workhorse, to map how songs like this move. Form: ragtime 16-bar and 32-bar forms. Listen for turnarounds borrowed from ragtime piano — it is the fingerprint of the style.

TO PLAY IT: set your tempo to the Piedmont Blues pocket, voice the chords cleanly, and let turnarounds borrowed from ragtime piano. Capo 2–4 for bright fingerstyle tone. (Song facts: title/artist/year are documented public records; the chart is an original study arrangement.)
